cues.text: Tens of thousands of chemicals are in commerce.
A few hundred have been tested for their effect on the developing nervous system.
The modern alternative to an animal study is to grow cortical neurons on a microelectrode array, and watch whether they organise themselves into a firing network.
It is faster.
It still costs days of culture, for every single compound.
So the binding question is not "is this chemical neurotoxic".
It is:
which ones go on the plate first?
First, the trap.
A chemical that simply kills the culture flattens every electrical measurement you can make.
Calling that neuroactive is how this kind of screen fools itself.
So the outcome is defined against viability.
A network effect counts only when it happens at least three-fold below the concentration that kills the cells.
Forty-nine compounds qualify.
Twenty-eight are inconclusive, and we publish them as inconclusive.
From a structure alone:
standardise it, fingerprint it, and find its nearest measured relatives among a hundred and two chemicals whose answer we already know.
Their outcomes, weighted by chemical similarity, become a score.
A conformal prediction set turns that score into a statement of confidence.
And when the nearest relative is too distant to say anything, the tool says nothing.
Test in the order the model recommends, and half the active compounds appear after thirty-two assays.
In a random order, fifty-one and a half.
Across two hundred independent splits, thirty-three to thirty-four.
Area under the curve:
zero point eight two eight on the pre-declared split, zero point seven seven six as the median of twenty others.
This is a retrospective evaluation, on a cohort the agency deliberately enriched with suspects.
We attacked it.
Then somebody else did.
A separate agent, which never saw our code, rebuilt the labels from the agency spreadsheet, and reimplemented the method from scratch.
Agreement:
five parts in ten to the seventeenth.
Then it shuffled the labels between chemical scaffolds, nine hundred and ninety-nine times, refitting everything on every shuffle.
Not one shuffle reached our result.
p equals zero point zero zero one.
The decision itself runs inside SciencePal.
The agent receives the measured analogues, twenty chemicals withheld from everything, and our scoring code — and not our answer.
Its chemical database was blocked.
It said so, found another route, and recovered a compound our own pipeline had thrown away:
the only one of the twenty it could call with confidence.
This does not tell you a chemical is safe.
A negative result in a dish does not exclude harm in development.
It tells you which plate to run on Monday.
The five it chose are a prediction.
One experiment would settle them.
